title: .revloop.json
description: Project configuration for revloop. Every field is optional; anything absent is auto-detected and shown in the resolved-configuration table with source=detected. Every key here has a consumer in commands/review-loop.md — a key with no consumer is a promise the procedure does not keep, so it is removed rather than left in place.

version.description: Config format version. An unknown major version aborts rather than degrading.

baseBranch.description: Null or absent: read from gh repo view --json defaultBranchRef.

branchPrefixes.description: Absent: derived from the repository's own commit subjects.

verify.description: Commands run before pushing. Shown in the resolved table BEFORE they run, and deliberately excluded from allowed-tools so the permission system always sees them.

verifyNotes.description: Which CI job the umbrella verify command does not reproduce, if any. The shape of this gap is universal; its answer differs per project and may be empty.

verifiedLabel.description: Label introducing the list of commands actually run, e.g. "Verified:".

trailers.description: {model} expands to the running model's name. No vendor address is stamped by default.

pr.description: The merge method is not configurable: the merge fence sends merge_method=merge, and it takes no arguments so that its command string never changes. Squash and rebase are not supported. CI cleanliness is likewise not configurable — the gate cannot be loosened from a file.

defaults.description: Defaults for the command flags. A flag always overrides its default. --merge and --auto are deliberately absent: this file comes from whatever repository you are working in, and a repository must not be able to turn on merging or to remove the two human confirmation points. Those two are settable by flag only, because the flag is the approval.

reviewer.description: Default for --reviewer on the pull-request loop only. Step 1 of that procedure aborts with reason=not-a-github-reviewer when the resolved name is a local-command reviewer, rather than falling through to the missing-trigger abort, which reports the wrong cause. A project driving both loops sets localReviewer as well.

localReviewer.description: Default for --reviewer on the local loop. It exists because `reviewer` is one key and the two loops need different values: every configuration written before the local loop points `reviewer` at a github-comment reviewer, and inheriting it would abort the local loop with reason=not-a-local-reviewer on every run until --reviewer was typed. Falling back to 'the only local reviewer defined' instead would be a guess, which is the thing an unknown --reviewer already refuses to make.

maxRounds.description: Circuit breaker on the number of rounds, for the pull-request loop only. It stays settable from config, unlike --accept-at, because it bounds spend rather than safety: raising it costs rounds and never merges anything.

localMaxRounds.description: Circuit breaker for the local loop. Separate from maxRounds because the two bound different things: a remote round spends a quota and a stretch of wall clock a person notices, while a local round spends tokens and nothing in the room displays that, so the cap is the only brake there is. It is NOT that a local round is quick: measured rounds run 5m27s to 8m39s, inside the remote reviewer's own range, so what differs is what a round spends and not how long it takes. Sharing one key let a remote-oriented value silently raise the local cap, which defeats the only limit that loop has. Built-in 5.

reviewers.description: Adds to, or overrides, the built-in presets. Every pattern here is used model-side only; none of it reaches a shell or a jq program. That is also the limit of what config can express: the wait fence watches reviews and comments unconditionally, and its list of non-terminal bot comments to drop lives inside the fence, so a reviewer that posts a preamble before its verdict needs a fence edit rather than a config key. A reviewer is one of two kinds and the required keys differ; see `kind`.

command.description: A subprocess command may not BEGIN WITH git — as a string prefix, with no exception for a longer name. The local command's own allowed-tools grants Bash(git:*), and docs/permissions.md states the model this rests on: Claude Code matches a COMMAND-STRING PREFIX against an allowlist. So every string starting with those three characters is covered by that grant and would run with no prompt at all, which is the one thing the not-pre-approved rule exists to prevent. `git push --force` is the shape that matters. TWO NARROWER SPELLINGS WERE TRIED AND BOTH LEAKED, in the same direction, because both asked where the WORD git ends when the grant does not ask that. `^\s*git(\s|$)` read only whitespace and end-of-string as ending it, so `git;rm -rf /`, `git&&rm -rf /`, `git&`, `git|tee`, `git>out`, `git<in` and `git"" push` all passed. `^\s*git($|[^A-Za-z0-9_.-])` closed those but still admitted gitlint, git-review and git.exe on the reasoning that they are different COMMANDS — true of the shell, and irrelevant to a matcher that compares strings. The prose in docs/permissions.md and in the procedure said 'may not begin with git' throughout; the implementation is now that sentence and nothing else. The cost is that a review command whose own name starts with git cannot be a subprocess reviewer. That is the correct side to err on: the alternative is a repository-supplied string running unprompted under a grant this command ships.

kind.description: Absent means github-comment, so every configuration written before this key existed keeps its meaning. github-comment is driven by posting a trigger to a pull request and reading GitHub; it requires botLogin. local-command is driven by running a review command on this machine; it requires invoke and command, and it may carry none of the GitHub-only keys, because nothing in the local loop posts a comment or filters a bot.

invoke.description: local-command only. subprocess runs `command` as a shell command line and reads its stdout; it is the only option for a review command whose host forbids model invocation, and it buys context isolation because the reviewer's file reads never enter the loop's own context. skill invokes `command` as a skill in this session.

command.description: local-command only. With invoke=skill this is a skill name and is narrowed further to ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*(:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*)?$. With invoke=subprocess it is a command line, so it is treated exactly as project.verify is: printed in the step-1 table before it runs and deliberately absent from allowed-tools, so the permission system always sees it. Any effort or focus argument the review command takes belongs in this string; there is no separate key for it, because the string is what the operator is shown and what the permission system matches.

requiresPr.description: local-command only. True when the review command resolves an open pull request itself and cannot run without one. The local loop opens none and has no gh grant, so it cannot check; it does not abort and does not guess. Step 1 asks the operator to confirm one exists, and step 7 refuses to read zero findings from such a reviewer as a clean round, because with no target and with a clean diff it returns the same nothing. An abort was the first design and made a shipped preset unreachable on the branches where it works.

trigger.description: Posted verbatim to GitHub. Control characters are rejected; a value already containing 'revloop:trigger' is rejected. A reviewer with no comment trigger cannot be driven: the procedure has only the comment path.

botLogin.description: Write it with the [bot] suffix. It is stripped before comparing against GraphQL, which omits it.

cleanPatterns.description: Anchor these at the start. A reviewer's clean phrase often has a varying tail, so equality tests break.

severityLevels.description: The reviewer's severity vocabulary, ORDERED MOST SEVERE FIRST. This ordering is the ladder --accept-at names: --accept-at <level> makes that level and everything below it acceptable, and leaves everything above it blocking. A reviewer that emits no severity has no key here, and --accept-at aborts with reason=no-severity-ladder rather than letting the loop invent a ladder for itself — the loop is the party obliged to fix the finding, so letting it rank its own findings would let it rank its way out of the work.

expectedLatency.description: Printed in the step-1 table. A verdict far below this range is usually a failure, not a review.

markerTolerated.description: Whether the reviewer still answers when the revloop marker is appended to the trigger. 'no' aborts in step 1: there is no fallback path.

status.description: Printed in the step-1 table and repeated in the final report when it is not 'verified'.
